variables.meaning: the heat absorbed or released by a substance, positive when the substance gains thermal energy and negative when it loses it
the heat capacity of a body of matter, the heat it absorbs or releases for a temperature change of 1 °C; it is extensive
the specific heat of a substance, the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of it by 1 °C; it is intensive
the mass of the substance that absorbs or releases the heat
the temperature change of the substance, its final temperature minus its initial temperature
the temperature of the substance before the heat is gained or lost
the temperature of the substance after the heat is gained or lost
the internal energy of a system, the total of all possible kinds of energy present in it
the change in the internal energy of a system
the work done on the system, positive when the surroundings do work on the system and negative when the system does work on the surroundings
the enthalpy of a system, the sum of its internal energy and the product of its pressure and volume
the enthalpy change of a process, equal to the heat flow when the process occurs at constant pressure with only expansion work
the pressure of the system, constant for the processes the enthalpy change describes
the volume of the system
the change in the volume of the system as it expands or contracts
the heat of a reaction under conditions of constant pressure
the standard enthalpy change, the enthalpy change for a process occurring under standard state conditions
the standard enthalpy of combustion, the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance burns completely under standard state conditions
the standard enthalpy of formation, the enthalpy change when exactly 1 mole of a substance forms from its elements in their most stable states under standard state conditions
the stoichiometric coefficient of a product or a reactant in the balanced equation

equations.condition: a body of matter that absorbs or releases heat q with no chemical reaction or phase change
a sample of one substance with no chemical reaction or phase change
no chemical reaction or phase change occurs, and the specific heat is treated as constant over the temperature range
an ideal calorimeter, in which all the heat transfer occurs between the two substances
the calorimeter absorbs no heat and exchanges none with the outside environment
a bomb calorimeter, with the heat absorbed by the products and the excess oxygen neglected
a process at constant pressure whose only work is caused by expansion or contraction
standard state conditions, with n the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation

glossary.definition: unit of heat or other energy; the amount of energy required to raise 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius; 1 cal is defined as 4.184 J
chemical reaction or physical change that absorbs heat
capacity to supply heat or do work
chemical reaction or physical change that releases heat
transfer of thermal energy between two bodies
extensive property of a body of matter that represents the quantity of heat required to increase its temperature by 1 degree Celsius (or 1 kelvin)
SI unit of energy; amount of energy used when a force of 1 newton moves an object 1 meter, 1 J = 1 kg m<sup>2</sup>/s<sup>2</sup> and 4.184 J = 1 cal
energy associated with an object's motion, equal to one-half the product of the object's mass and the square of its velocity, $\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$ (where m = mass and v = velocity)
energy of a particle or system of particles derived from relative position, composition, or condition
intensive property of a substance that represents the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of the substance by 1 degree Celsius (or 1 kelvin)
intensive property of matter that is a quantitative measure of “hotness” and “coldness”
kinetic energy associated with the random motion of atoms and molecules
study of measuring the amount of heat absorbed or released during a chemical reaction or a physical change
energy transfer due to changes in external, macroscopic variables such as pressure and volume; or causing matter to move against an opposing force
device designed to measure the energy change for processes occurring under conditions of constant volume; commonly used for reactions involving solid and gaseous reactants or products
device used to measure the amount of heat absorbed or released in a chemical or physical process
process of measuring the amount of heat involved in a chemical or physical process
unit used for quantifying energy provided by digestion of foods, defined as 1000 cal or 1 kcal
all matter other than the system being studied
portion of matter undergoing a chemical or physical change being studied
area of science that deals with the relationships between heat, work, and all forms of energy associated with chemical and physical processes
sum of a system’s internal energy and the mathematical product of its pressure and volume
heat released or absorbed by a system under constant pressure during a chemical or physical process
work done as a system expands or contracts against external pressure
internal energy of a system changes due to heat flow in or out of the system or work done on or by the system
if a process can be represented as the sum of several steps, the enthalpy change of the process equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the steps
compound composed only of hydrogen and carbon; the major component of fossil fuels
total of all possible kinds of energy present in a substance or substances
heat released when one mole of a compound undergoes complete combustion under standard conditions
enthalpy change of a chemical reaction in which 1 mole of a pure substance is formed from its elements in their most stable states under standard state conditions

set of physical conditions as accepted as common reference conditions for reporting thermodynamic properties; 1 bar of pressure, and solutions at 1 molar concentrations, usually at a temperature of 298.15 K
property depending only on the state of a system, and not the path taken to reach that state
